section_summary: This section consists of six General Headquarters, United States Army Forces, Pacific, press inventories prepared for Ambassador Edwin W. Pauley’s reparations mission and completed on 1 December 1945. They assess Japan’s postwar shipbuilding, telecommunications, radio, aluminum and magnesium, electric-power, iron-and-steel, coal, and petroleum industries, emphasizing capacity, war damage, raw-material and labor shortages, and estimated peacetime requirements. The reports also describe former Japanese industrial facilities and resource sources in Korea, Taiwan, Manchuria, northern China, and the Dutch East Indies.

people.name: Edwin W. Pauley
people.role: Ambassador and chief of the United States reparations mission in Japan

people.name: Morris N. Lipp
people.role: Chief of the Shipbuilding Branch, Industrial Division, Economic and Scientific Section, SCAP; an Army captain on leave from his civilian position as city engineer of Miami, Florida

subfiles.title: Industrial Inventory No. 2: The Shipbuilding Industry
subfiles.from: General Headquarters, United States Army Forces, Pacific, Public Relations Office
subfiles.about: An assessment of Japan’s surviving steel and wooden shipbuilding and ship-repair capacity.
subfiles.summary: The inventory reports that Japanese yards had ways for the simultaneous construction of 176 steel ships and as many as 2,000 small wooden vessels, although shortages of labor, materials, and equipment sharply limited actual use. It classifies steel-ship ways by vessel size and records 63 drydocks and four floating drydocks. Capt. Morris N. Lipp supervised the inventory.

subfiles.title: Industrial Inventory No. 3: Telephone and Radio Equipment Industry
subfiles.from: General Headquarters, United States Army Forces, Pacific, Public Relations Office
subfiles.about: A survey of Japan’s telephone system and its manufacturing capacity for telephones, radios, tubes, and electronic components.
subfiles.summary: The report inventories 22 telephone-equipment factories and estimates production capacity after dispersed machinery and labor are restored. It assesses heavy wartime damage to telephone service, particularly in Osaka, Tokyo, Hiroshima, and Nagasaki, while noting Kyoto’s very light losses. The radio section describes assembly and tube-manufacturing capacity, the tube shortage, surviving civilian receivers, clandestine shortwave sets, and the destruction of military electronic production capacity.

subfiles.title: Industrial Inventory No. 4: Aluminum and Magnesium
subfiles.from: General Headquarters, United States Army Forces, Pacific, Public Relations Office
subfiles.about: A survey of Japanese alumina, aluminum, magnesium, and other nonferrous-metal production facilities and stocks.
subfiles.summary: The inventory details alumina and aluminum plants in Japan and former Japanese-controlled territories, their rated capacities, war damage, and sharply reduced wartime output. Aluminum production collapsed after Japan exhausted its bauxite and Allied operations severed imports from Bintan Island following the invasion of Leyte. It also records magnesium production and stocks and lists factories producing copper, aluminum, brass, magnesium, lead, and tin goods.

subfiles.title: Industrial Inventory No. 5: Electric Power
subfiles.from: General Headquarters, United States Army Forces, Pacific, Public Relations Office
subfiles.about: A statistical inventory of Japan’s hydroelectric, thermal, and steam-electric generating plants.
subfiles.summary: As of 20 November 1945, the report counts 1,898 generating plants or stations with maximum capacity of 13,465,488 kilowatts. It divides the system among hydroelectric, thermal, and steam facilities and further distinguishes public-utility and privately owned plants. It also classifies plants by generating capacity and notes facilities still under construction or enlargement.

subfiles.title: Industrial Inventory No. 6: Iron and Steel
subfiles.from: General Headquarters, United States Army Forces, Pacific, Public Relations Office
subfiles.about: An inventory of Japan’s pig-iron, ingot-steel, rolling-mill, and special-steel capacity and estimated peacetime requirements.
subfiles.summary: The report enumerates Japan’s pig-iron and steel plants, blast furnaces, open-hearth and electric furnaces, and rolling mills, comparing rated capacity with actual wartime production. It analyzes imports and domestic availability of iron ore, coal, manganese, scrap, and other inputs and calculates material requirements for postwar output. The final portion argues that wartime special-steel capacity greatly exceeded likely peacetime needs and records large stocks remaining at the war’s end.

subfiles.title: Industrial Inventory No. 7: Coal and Petroleum
subfiles.from: General Headquarters, United States Army Forces, Pacific, Public Relations Office
subfiles.about: A survey of Japan’s coal mining, coal-carbonization, coke, city-gas, and domestic petroleum industries.
subfiles.summary: The coal section compares output in Kyushu, Hokkaido, and Honshu, projects production through 1949, and identifies shortages of materials and labor following the repatriation of Korean miners. It also values the mining industry and inventories carbonization benches, coke ovens, and city-gas and steel-plant processing capacity before and after war damage. The petroleum section traces domestic crude production and describes output from the Akita, Niigata, Yamagata, and Hokkaido districts, noting that drilling equipment and personnel had been transferred to captured Dutch East Indies oil fields.
